NEW DELHI, India (CNN) -- While many now recognize the scientific explanation for a solar eclipse, the phenomenon is still marked with tradition and sometimes suspicion in Hindu-majority India. People test the "sky watching telescope" at the Gujarat Council of Science City in India. The "exceptionally long" eclipse that will cross half the planet Wednesday will be able to be seen by virtually all of the population of China and India. For beggars in India, the occasion means an extra day of receiving alms and food. The panhandler in Sandeep Jaggi's neighborhood normally visits the block every week on Tuesdays and Saturdays, as well as the days of a new and full moon. And because his patrons mark an eclipse with alms-giving, prayers and bathing, he rarely misses the chance to meet them on this day as well. "It's a family tradition and I follow it," says 34-year-old Jaggi. He will fill the beggar's small steel pail with mustard oil and coins and his disheveled sash with lentils. For others in the country, the eclipse is not a reason to celebrate, but a more ominous phenomenon. Send us your photos of the eclipse . Most pregnant women hope to avoid giving birth during an eclipse. "None of the expectant mothers under my treatment are willing to have deliveries on Wednesday," Shivani Sachdev Gour, a gynecologist at New Delhi's Fortis La Femme hospital, told CNN. In fact, there are critically ill patients who do not want to be in the hospital on the day of the eclipse, she said. Indian astrologers even advise expectant mothers to stay indoors when this celestial event occurs. "It may not cause any physical harm to the baby, but it may affect the child's overall personality," said R.K. Sharma, who describes himself as a "remedial astrologer." A solar eclipse, he says, weakens the sun god temporarily because of an encounter with dragon Rahu and leaves some cascading results everywhere. "Bathing in holy rivers and ponds during this time thus helps protect health and develop positivism and greater will power," he explained. About 1.5 million people are expected at one such pond -- the Brahmsarovar, or the pool of Hindu god Brahma -- in northern India on Wednesday. "They offer prayers to the sun god and take holy dips during an eclipse," said Ashok Kumar Bansal, the sub-divisional magistrate of Kurukshetra, an ancient Hindu city. But the century's longest total solar eclipse is not just about the dragon-sun combat, it also means business for some. Travel firms in India have plans in place to cash in on the phenomenon. Cox and Kings India has a planeload of eclipse watchers heading for the eastern state of Bihar, one of the most preferred locations for sighting the event. The plane will hover over Gaya in Bihar and return to New Delhi the same day, company spokesman Thomas C. Thottathil told CNN. Passengers were given two options: to book a "sunside" seat facing the eclipse for about $1,640, or reserve an "earthside" seat for about $610, Thottathil added. "And it's a sold out flight now!" he said.

# Solar Eclipse Stirs Tradition, Superstition, and Commerce in India

**NEW DELHI, India (CNN)** — Although the scientific explanation for solar eclipses is widely understood today, the phenomenon continues to be steeped in tradition—and, at times, apprehension—across Hindu-majority India.

Visitors test the "sky-watching telescope" at the Gujarat Council of Science City. The "exceptionally long" eclipse set to sweep across half the globe on Wednesday will be visible to nearly the entire populations of China and India alike.

For India's beggars, the occasion promises an additional day of alms and sustenance. The panhandler who frequents Sandeep Jaggi's neighborhood typically makes his rounds every Tuesday and Saturday, as well as on new and full moon days. Since Jaggi's household marks eclipses with charity, prayer, and ritual bathing, he rarely lets the occasion pass without greeting the man once more.

"It's a family tradition, and I uphold it," says Jaggi, 34. He plans to fill the beggar's small steel pail with mustard oil and coins, and his frayed sash with lentils.

**Send us your photos of the eclipse.**

For others across the country, however, the eclipse inspires not celebration but foreboding. Most expectant mothers, for instance, hope to avoid giving birth during the event. "None of the expectant mothers under my care wish to deliver on Wednesday," Dr. Shivani Sachdev Gour, a gynecologist at New Delhi's Fortis La Femme Hospital, told CNN. She noted that even some critically ill patients have expressed a desire to avoid the hospital altogether on eclipse day.

Indian astrologers, too, counsel pregnant women to remain indoors during the celestial event. "It may not cause any physical harm to the baby, but it could affect the child's overall temperament," explained R.K. Sharma, who identifies himself as a "remedial astrologer." According to Sharma, a solar eclipse temporarily weakens the sun god following his mythological clash with the serpent Rahu, unleashing ripple effects throughout the world. "Bathing in holy rivers and ponds during this period helps safeguard one's health and cultivates positivity and inner strength," he added.

An estimated 1.5 million people are expected to gather at one such sacred site—the Brahmsarovar, or "Pool of Brahma"—in northern India on Wednesday. "They offer prayers to the sun god and take holy dips during the eclipse," said Ashok Kumar Bansal, sub-divisional magistrate of Kurukshetra, an ancient city of religious significance.

Yet the century's longest total solar eclipse is not solely a story of celestial mythology—it has also become a lucrative business opportunity. Travel companies across India are moving swiftly to capitalize on the event. Cox and Kings India, for one, has chartered a plane full of eclipse enthusiasts bound for the eastern state of Bihar, among the most sought-after vantage points for viewing the spectacle.

The aircraft will hover above Gaya in Bihar before returning to New Delhi the same day, said company spokesman Thomas C. Thottathil. Passengers were offered a choice between a "sunside" seat facing the eclipse, priced at roughly $1,640, or an "earthside" seat for about $610.

"And it's a sold-out flight now!" Thottathil exclaimed.

# Solar Eclipse Sparks Mix of Science and Superstition in India

**NEW DELHI, India (CNN)** — Even as scientific understanding of solar eclipses has become widespread, this astronomical event continues to carry deep cultural weight—and occasional wariness—in a country where Hindus form the majority.

Visitors try out the "sky watching telescope" at Gujarat's Council of Science City. This week's eclipse, notable for its unusually long duration and path crossing half the globe, will be visible to nearly everyone living in China and India come Wednesday.

For India's homeless population, this natural event translates into extra charity. Take the beggar who frequents Sandeep Jaggi's street—typically appearing only on Tuesdays, Saturdays, and lunar transition days. Since Jaggi's community treats eclipses as occasions for donations, purification rituals, and prayer, he makes a point of showing up on this day too.

"It's something my family has always done, and I keep it going," explains Jaggi, age 34. His plan: fill the man's metal container with coins and oil, then tuck lentils into his worn cloth belt.

Not everyone views the eclipse so warmly, however—for some, it signals something far more threatening.

*Share your eclipse photos with us.*

Take expectant mothers, many of whom actively try to schedule around such events. According to Dr. Shivani Sachdev Gour, a gynecologist practicing at Fortis La Femme in New Delhi, "None of the expectant mothers under my treatment are willing to have deliveries on Wednesday." She adds that even severely ill patients sometimes request to avoid hospital stays specifically during eclipse hours.

Astrology practitioners in India go so far as to recommend pregnant women remain indoors throughout the celestial event. R.K. Sharma, who identifies as a "remedial astrologer," explains: "It may not cause any physical harm to the baby, but it may affect the child's overall personality." According to Sharma's account, the eclipse temporarily diminishes the sun deity's power through a clash with the mythical serpent Rahu, triggering ripple effects across the world. He recommends ritual bathing in sacred waters as protection, saying it "helps protect health and develop positivism and greater will power."

Roughly 1.5 million devotees are anticipated to gather at Brahmsarovar—a pond named for the Hindu creator god Brahma—in northern India this Wednesday. Ashok Kumar Bansal, sub-divisional magistrate overseeing the historic city of Kurukshetra, notes that visitors "offer prayers to the sun god and take holy dips during an eclipse."

Beyond mythology and ritual, though, this century's lengthiest total solar eclipse also represents a commercial opportunity. Several Indian travel companies have crafted special packages around the event.

Cox and Kings India, for instance, has fully booked a flight carrying eclipse enthusiasts to Bihar in eastern India—widely considered prime viewing territory. According to company representative Thomas C. Thottathil, the aircraft will circle above Gaya before returning to New Delhi that same day.

Two ticket tiers were offered: roughly $1,640 for a "sunside" seat with direct eclipse views, or about $610 for an "earthside" alternative. Thottathil confirmed enthusiastically, "And it's a sold out flight now!"

# Solar Eclipse to Sweep Across Asia, Reviving Ancient Traditions Amid Modern Science

An upcoming solar eclipse is set to captivate nearly half the globe on Wednesday, with its shadow stretching across a vast swath of the planet and reaching the densely populated nations of China and India. Together, these two countries are home to nearly a third of the world's population, meaning billions of people will have the opportunity to witness this rare celestial event, even if only partially in some regions.

While modern astronomy has long demystified the mechanics of solar eclipses—the moon passing between the Earth and the sun, temporarily blocking its light—the event continues to hold profound cultural and spiritual significance in India. Despite widespread access to scientific education and near-universal understanding of the phenomenon's natural causes, deep-rooted traditions and superstitions persist, weaving themselves into the fabric of daily life during these celestial occurrences.

## A Day of Giving

For many in India, the eclipse is not just a moment of astronomical wonder but also an occasion for charity. Beggars across the country often see a noticeable uptick in generosity on eclipse days, as families uphold long-standing customs of giving alms. Sandeep Jaggi, a patron who continues a tradition passed down through generations, is one such example. Following practices instilled by his family, he distributes coins and food to those in need, believing that acts of charity during the eclipse carry special merit and can help ward off any inauspicious energy associated with the event.

## Caution in the Delivery Room

The eclipse's influence extends even into the medical field, where lingering beliefs about potential harm continue to shape practical decisions. Gynecologist Shivani Sachdev Gour is among many doctors who consciously avoid scheduling deliveries or non-emergency hospital procedures on the day of an eclipse. This practice reflects a broader concern shared by expectant mothers and their families, who fear that exposure to the eclipse could negatively affect both mother and child. Despite the absence of scientific evidence supporting these claims, the tradition remains strong enough to influence hospital scheduling and patient behavior, illustrating how deeply embedded these beliefs are in everyday medical practice.

## Mythology Behind the Fear

To understand the roots of these enduring superstitions, astrologer R.K. Sharma offers insight into the ancient mythology that continues to shape perceptions of the eclipse. According to traditional Hindu belief, the phenomenon is linked to the legend of Rahu, a mythical dragon or demon who is said to swallow the sun, causing it to weaken and darken temporarily. This celestial battle between the sun god and Rahu is thought to release negative energies that can affect human well-being.

To counteract these effects, Sharma recommends specific protective rituals, most notably bathing in holy rivers such as the Ganges. This purification practice is believed to cleanse the body and spirit of any harmful influences unleashed during the eclipse, restoring balance and protecting against misfortune. Such rituals, passed down through countless generations, remain widely observed even today, serving as a bridge between ancient mythology and contemporary life.

## Tradition and Science in Coexistence

As the eclipse approaches, it serves as a fascinating reminder of how scientific knowledge and cultural tradition can coexist within the same society. While astronomers and educated citizens alike understand the eclipse as a natural, predictable celestial event, the pull of ancestral customs and spiritual beliefs remains powerful. From charitable giving to medical scheduling and purification rituals, the eclipse continues to be a moment where science and superstition intersect, offering a glimpse into the rich cultural tapestry that shapes how millions experience this extraordinary astronomical phenomenon.

# The Eclipse That Divides Science and Superstition

This week, an extraordinary celestial event unfolded across Asia—one of the longest total solar eclipses in over a century, visible to the combined populations of nearly 2.5 billion people across China and India. While astronomers and scientists celebrated the rare opportunity to study the sun's corona and other astronomical phenomena, on the ground in India, the eclipse revealed something far more complex: a society caught between the empirical certainties of modern science and the enduring pull of ancient tradition.

For millions of devout Hindus, the eclipse is not merely an astronomical curiosity but a moment charged with spiritual significance. Religious texts and generations of oral tradition have long characterized eclipses as inauspicious periods—times when malevolent celestial forces are believed to hold sway. In response, many devout Indians engaged in centuries-old rituals meant to ward off ill fortune. Almsgiving to beggars saw a notable increase, rooted in the belief that charity during these dark celestial moments could offset negative cosmic energies and bring spiritual merit. Temples across the country reported surges in prayer offerings, while some devotees fasted or avoided eating altogether during the eclipse's duration, adhering to age-old beliefs that food prepared or consumed during this time could become contaminated by harmful rays.

Perhaps the most striking illustration of tradition's grip, however, emerged not in temples or streets, but in hospitals and maternity wards throughout the country. In a phenomenon that reveals just how deeply embedded these beliefs are—even among those trained in modern medicine—numerous expectant mothers and their physicians made a conscious decision to reschedule planned deliveries and cesarean sections to avoid the eclipse window entirely.

The reasoning behind this practice traces back to astrological beliefs suggesting that a child born during a solar eclipse may be marked by negative personality traits, misfortune, or an inauspicious life path. Some traditions hold that the celestial "shadow" cast during the eclipse can somehow imprint itself upon a newborn's fate, influencing everything from temperament to future success. Families consulted astrologers to determine optimal birth timing, and some medical practitioners—responding to patient requests and, in some cases, their own personal convictions—proved willing to accommodate these concerns by adjusting delivery schedules.

This practice stands in stark contrast to established medical and scientific consensus. There is no credible scientific evidence suggesting that solar eclipses pose any physical risk to unborn children or that timing of birth in relation to celestial events has any bearing on a child's future characteristics or wellbeing. Obstetricians operating from a purely evidence-based framework note that the sun's temporary obstruction has no measurable physiological effect on pregnancy, labor, or infant development.

Yet the persistence of this practice underscores a broader truth about the relationship between science and culture in India and beyond: scientific literacy and traditional belief systems often coexist, sometimes in tension, sometimes in surprising harmony. Even as India has become a global leader in space exploration and technology, ancient customs continue to shape everyday decisions—including deeply personal and consequential ones like the timing of a child's birth.

This duality is not necessarily viewed as contradictory by those who practice it. For many, adhering to astrological guidance alongside modern medical care reflects a holistic approach to life—one that honors ancestral wisdom while still accessing contemporary healthcare. Whether driven by genuine belief, family pressure, cultural identity, or simple precaution, the choice to avoid eclipse-timed births represents a fascinating intersection where celestial mechanics, religious cosmology, and modern medicine converge, offering a window into how deeply history and heritage continue to inform the present, even in an age of scientific advancement.

# New Delhi: The Capital Heart of India

New Delhi stands as the capital city of India, serving as the political, administrative, and cultural nerve center of one of the world's most populous nations. Nestled within the larger metropolitan area of Delhi, this vibrant city seamlessly blends ancient heritage with modern governance, making it a fascinating study in contrasts.

## A City of Historical Significance

New Delhi was designed and constructed during the British colonial era, with construction beginning in 1911 and the city being formally inaugurated in 1931. Architects Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker envisioned a grand imperial capital, and their legacy remains visible today in structures like the Rashtrapati Bhavan (Presidential Palace), India Gate, and the wide, tree-lined avenues of Lutyens' Delhi.

## The Seat of Indian Democracy

As India's capital, New Delhi houses the country's most important governmental institutions. The Parliament House, Supreme Court, and numerous ministries are located here, making it the epicenter of decision-making for a nation of over 1.4 billion people. Foreign embassies and diplomatic missions also cluster in the city, underscoring its role in India's international relations.

## Cultural and Economic Hub

Beyond politics, New Delhi serves as a gateway to India's rich cultural tapestry. The city hosts numerous museums, historical monuments, and UNESCO World Heritage Sites, including the Qutub Minar and Humayun's Tomb. Its bustling markets, from the traditional Chandni Chowk to modern shopping complexes, reflect the economic dynamism driving India's growth.

## Conclusion

New Delhi represents far more than just India's administrative capital—it embodies the nation's journey from ancient civilization to modern global power. As India continues to assert itself on the world stage, New Delhi remains at the forefront, balancing tradition with progress in one of Asia's most dynamic urban centers.

# India Prepares for Rare Celestial Spectacle as Total Solar Eclipse Sparks Mix of Scientific Wonder and Ancient Traditions

**New Delhi, India** — Millions across India are preparing for an upcoming total solar eclipse, an event that has ignited a fascinating dual response nationwide: cutting-edge scientific enthusiasm colliding with centuries-old cultural practices.

## Scientists Urge Public to Embrace the Phenomenon

Astronomers and educational institutions across the country are mobilizing to make the eclipse a teachable moment. The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and several planetariums have announced special viewing events, distributing certified solar filter glasses and setting up telescopes in public parks and school grounds.

"This is a golden opportunity to inspire the next generation of scientists," said Dr. Anjali Rao, an astrophysicist affiliated with a prominent Indian research institute. "A total solar eclipse allows us to study the sun's corona in ways that aren't possible any other time. We're encouraging families, especially children, to observe safely and understand the mechanics behind this cosmic alignment."

Educational campaigns have flooded social media and television, emphasizing eye safety and dispelling myths. Schools in several states have organized special assemblies where physics teachers demonstrate, using simple models, how the moon's shadow falls upon the Earth.

Tech-savvy citizens are also gearing up, with astronomy clubs organizing live-streaming sessions and photography workshops to capture the diamond ring effect and Baily's beads — phenomena visible only during totality.

## Traditional Practices Persist in Many Communities

Alongside the scientific excitement, deeply rooted cultural and religious customs continue to shape how many Indians, particularly in rural and traditional communities, approach the eclipse.

In Hindu tradition, solar eclipses—known as "Surya Grahan"—are often viewed through a mythological lens, tied to the legend of the demon Rahu swallowing the sun. Many temples across the country will temporarily close their doors during the eclipse period, with priests conducting purification rituals before reopening.

"During Grahan, we follow practices passed down through generations," explained Meera Devi, a resident of a small town in Uttar Pradesh. "We avoid cooking or eating during the eclipse, and pregnant women in our family stay indoors, as it's believed exposure could affect the unborn child. After the eclipse ends, we bathe and pray to cleanse ourselves."

Fasting is common in many households during the eclipse window, with observant Hindus abstaining from food and water until the celestial event concludes. Ritual baths, often in sacred rivers like the Ganges, are also expected to see a surge in visitors both before and after the eclipse, as devotees seek spiritual purification.

Pregnant women, in particular, remain a focal point of these traditions. Many are advised by family elders to stay indoors, avoid sharp objects, and refrain from certain activities—beliefs rooted in generations-old folklore about potential effects on childbirth.

## A Nation Bridging Old and New

Despite the apparent contrast between scientific rationalism and traditional beliefs, many Indians find ways to honor both. Some families report watching the eclipse through certified glasses while also observing customary fasting practices, seeing no contradiction between scientific curiosity and cultural respect.

"My grandmother will perform her rituals, and I'll be outside with my telescope," said Rohan Mehta, a college student in Mumbai. "It's not really a conflict—it's just two different ways of experiencing something remarkable."

Government health officials have also weighed in, particularly regarding pregnant women, reassuring the public that there is no scientific evidence linking eclipses to complications in pregnancy, while respecting individuals' rights to observe personal or religious customs.

As the countdown continues, India stands poised to experience the eclipse through its characteristic blend of ancient reverence and modern scientific pursuit—a reflection of the country's broader relationship with tradition and progress.

*Local viewing events and safety guidelines can be found through regional science centers and ISRO's official channels.*

# In India, Ancient Beliefs and Modern Science Collide as Solar Eclipse Sweeps the Nation

**NEW DELHI** — As the moon began its slow creep across the sun, temples across India shuttered their doors, pregnant women retreated indoors, and millions set aside cooked food believed to turn toxic under the darkened sky. The scene, repeated for centuries, once again illustrated the striking coexistence of ancient tradition and modern rationalism in a nation home to both cutting-edge space missions and deeply rooted astrological practices.

For many Hindus, a solar eclipse — or "Surya Grahan" — is far more than an astronomical event. It's considered a period of cosmic vulnerability, governed by mythology dating back thousands of years.

"According to our shastras, the eclipse occurs when the demon Rahu swallows the sun," said Pandit Ramesh Sharma, a Delhi-based astrologer who has spent over three decades studying Vedic traditions. "This is not merely superstition — it is a time when negative energies are at their peak. We advise people to chant mantras, avoid eating, and stay indoors, particularly those who are pregnant or unwell."

Across the country, temples closed their doors hours before the eclipse began, reopening only after purification rituals were performed. Devotees took ritual baths in the Ganges and other sacred rivers, believing the waters could cleanse negative cosmic influences. Many households covered their windows, refusing to let the eclipse's rays touch their food or living spaces.

Pregnant women, in particular, are often advised to remain indoors entirely during the eclipse. Tradition holds that exposure could harm the unborn child — a belief that, despite modern medical understanding, remains deeply ingrained in many communities.

"My mother-in-law insisted I stay in a dark room with the curtains drawn," said Priya Nair, a 28-year-old expectant mother in Mumbai. "She said if I stepped outside, the baby could be born with a defect. I don't necessarily believe it, but I didn't want to take any chances or cause tension in the family."

Doctors, however, have long pushed back against such beliefs, stressing that there is no scientific evidence linking eclipses to birth defects or contaminated food.

"There is absolutely no medical basis for the idea that an eclipse can harm a pregnancy or spoil food," said Dr. Anjali Mehta, an OB-GYN based in Bangalore. "What we do worry about is eye damage from looking directly at the sun without proper protection. That is the real health concern — not mythology. Every year, we see patients with retinal damage because they watched the eclipse without eclipse glasses."

Indeed, ophthalmologists across the country used the event as an opportunity for public health messaging, urging citizens to use certified solar filters or indirect viewing methods rather than relying on sunglasses or exposed film, which offer little real protection.

Yet even as hospitals issued warnings about UV exposure, astrologers continued to receive a steady stream of calls from anxious citizens seeking guidance on rituals and precautions.

"People call me not just from India, but from the U.S., the UK, wherever there is a large Indian diaspora," Sharma said. "They want to know: should I fast? Should I avoid travel? Is this a good time to start a new business? The eclipse touches every part of life, according to our beliefs."

This tension between tradition and science is not new in India, a country where ISRO — the nation's space agency — has landed spacecraft on the moon, even as astrology remains a multi-million dollar industry consulted by everyone from farmers to politicians before making major decisions.

For sociologist Dr. Kavita Rao, the coexistence of these worldviews reflects something deeper about Indian identity itself.

"India doesn't see science and spirituality as inherently contradictory," Rao explained. "You can have a family where the son is a rocket scientist and the grandmother is performing eclipse rituals in the same house, and there's no real conflict. It's about honoring both empirical knowledge and cultural heritage."

As the shadow of the moon moved on and the sun re-emerged, temple bells rang out once more, signaling that the period of cosmic disturbance had passed. Cooked food that had been set aside was discarded. Fresh meals were prepared. And life, guided by a blend of faith and fact, resumed its normal rhythm — until the next eclipse draws the nation's gaze skyward once again.

## The Medical Perspective

At Fortis Hospital in New Delhi, Dr. Priya Sharma, a gynecologist with over 15 years of experience, spent the days leading up to the eclipse fielding anxious calls from pregnant patients.

"I probably answered the same question 50 times this week: 'Doctor, should I stay indoors during the eclipse? Will it harm my baby?'" Dr. Sharma said, shaking her head with a mix of patience and frustration. "There is absolutely no scientific evidence that solar eclipses affect fetal development. But the belief runs so deep that some of my patients wanted to schedule C-sections around the eclipse timing."

Traditional beliefs hold that pregnant women should avoid stepping outside during an eclipse, avoid using sharp objects, and refrain from eating, fearing birth defects or complications. Dr. Sharma noted that while she respects her patients' cultural backgrounds, she makes it a point to gently educate them.

"I tell them, look, astronauts have studied eclipses up close. NASA has scientists standing outside watching these events. If there was any radiation danger beyond looking directly at the sun without protection, we would know," she explained. "But I also understand—these beliefs aren't just superstition to families, they're inherited wisdom passed down through generations. My job is to add scientific information, not dismiss their culture entirely."

## The Astrological Angle

Just a few kilometers away, astrologer Pandit Rajesh Trivedi's phone hadn't stopped ringing for days. His small office near Karol Bagh was filled with clients seeking guidance on everything from business decisions to marriage compatibility, all recalibrated around the eclipse's astrological significance.

"Surya Grahan is a time of immense cosmic energy shifting," Trivedi explained, referencing the Sanskrit term for solar eclipse. "In Vedic astrology, this is when Rahu and Ketu—the shadow planets—create disturbances in the natural order. People want to know how this affects their kundali, their birth chart."

Trivedi advised clients to avoid starting new ventures, signing important documents, or making major life decisions during the eclipse period, known as *Sutak Kaal*, which traditionally begins several hours before the visible eclipse.

"Temples close, cooking is avoided, some people fast entirely," he said. "Science tells you what is happening physically. Astrology tells you what is happening energetically. Both can be true simultaneously."

When asked about the tension with modern scientific understanding, Trivedi was diplomatic. "I'm not against science. My own son is an engineer! But this knowledge system has guided Indian civilization for thousands of years. Why should modern astronomy erase thousands of years of observation and wisdom?"

## Eclipse Tourism Boom

Perhaps the most surprising angle emerged from the tourism industry, where the eclipse has become big business.

"We've seen a 300% increase in bookings for eclipse-viewing packages," said Ananya Reddy, spokesperson for Cosmic Journeys Travel, a company specializing in astronomical tourism. "We took groups to Rajasthan and parts of Gujarat where the eclipse path offered the best viewing angles."

Reddy's company catered to a curious mix of clients: hardcore astronomy enthusiasts wanting to witness the celestial mechanics firsthand, and families seeking to combine spiritual eclipse rituals with travel experiences.

"It's interesting—we get scientists and skeptics who want solar filters and telescopes, standing right next to families who want to perform specific pujas during totality, or who insist on being near a holy river during the eclipse for purification rituals," Reddy said. "We've had to train our tour guides to speak both languages—the astronomical facts and the traditional customs—because our clients want both explained."

The company offered package deals including protective eclipse glasses, telescope viewing sessions with astronomy experts, alongside options for ritual baths at pilgrimage sites and consultations with astrologers for those wanting to understand the event's spiritual implications.

"Business-wise, it doesn't matter if someone believes in astrology or pure astronomy," Reddy added with a laugh. "Everyone wants to see the eclipse. We just make sure they see it safely, whatever their beliefs."

As the moon's shadow moved across the subcontinent and eventually departed Indian skies, it left behind not answers, but a continued, uniquely Indian conversation—one where telescopes and temple bells, science and sacred texts, continue to coexist under the same sky.
